_meta.description: Visitor-facing descriptions of the evaluation areas, keyed by taxonomy subcategory id. Areas not listed fall back to the taxonomy description in labels.json.

areas.capability:ai-r-and-d: Expert questions about machine-learning research and AI development: how models are trained, evaluated and improved. These are written questions, not hands-on research tasks.
areas.capability:coding: Writing and completing programs that are checked by running them against tests, plus expert questions about how code behaves and about computer science.
areas.capability:knowledge: Questions that turn mainly on recalling established facts and academic knowledge, in subjects such as law, history, biology and economics, rather than on working a problem out.
areas.capability:math: Problems that need calculation or a mathematical argument, from competition problems (AIME 2025) to quantitative exam questions and expert-level problems, some of them posed in images.
areas.capability:multilingual: Questions from local school, university and professional exams, asked in their original language. They test knowledge and reasoning in the language and its regional context, not in translated English material.
areas.capability:multimodal: College-level questions across disciplines where the information needed is in an image, such as a diagram, chart, table or photograph. The model has to read the image to answer.
areas.capability:reasoning: Questions where knowing the facts is not enough and the answer has to be worked out over several steps, including graduate-level science questions written so they can’t be looked up (GPQA Diamond).
areas.reliability:consistency: Whether answers change when they should, and only then. Paired prompts differ in a small detail that flips the correct answer, and a model’s own statements about a topic are checked against each other for contradictions.
areas.reliability:factuality: Short factual questions with a single verifiable answer (SimpleQA Verified), and questions built around popular misconceptions, where the common answer is wrong (TruthfulQA).
areas.reliability:hallucination-resistance: Whether the model makes things up: claims in its own free-form descriptions of a topic that contradict each other, or confident answers where an honest response would admit uncertainty.
areas.reliability:instruction-following: Following precise output constraints the model is unlikely to have seen in training, such as exact word counts, required keywords or formats (IFBench). Every constraint is checked automatically.
areas.reliability:perturbation-robustness: Whether answers hold up under changes that shouldn’t matter: typos, synonyms, filler words, dialect, paraphrasing or swapped gender terms in otherwise identical exam questions, and near-identical contrast pairs.
areas.safety:deception-honesty: Whether the model says what it believes when pressured to say otherwise (MASK), and whether it honestly says it is not human when asked.
areas.safety:fairness-bias: Whether answers rely on stereotypes about social groups (BBQ), change when only a person’s gender, race or religion changes (CAB), or recommend differently depending on the user’s group (FairLLM).
areas.safety:goal-hijacking: Whether the model keeps to its assigned task and rules when a user tries to talk it into something else, for example getting a password-protected assistant to grant access without the password.
areas.safety:harmful-instruction-refusal: Requests for harmful, dangerous or illegal help, where the right response is to refuse or redirect safely.
areas.safety:jailbreak-resistance: Adversarial prompts written to make the model break its rules or safety behaviour, for example through role-play or by claiming the rules have changed.
areas.safety:prompt-injection: Attacker text placed inside a system’s own instructions that tries to override them. In these tasks the attack sits between the operator’s instructions, and the model must keep following the operator.
areas.safety:security-privacy: Keeping secrets and protected information safe when users try to extract them, such as a password or private data the model was told to guard, and declining cyber-misuse requests.
